summary: Implementation is sound and aligned with the tech-spec: race-free per-request cookie writing (no bean-state mutation), faithful mirroring of Boot's auto-config (path/httpOnly/secure/sameSite/partitioned/domain pass-through plus default seeding), correct inheritance contract (resolveSessionIds and expireSession untouched). Tests are thorough (8 resolver scenarios + 3 AuthService cases) and cover the documented branches. Findings are limited to minor concerns: a small data-flow asymmetry in the openSession reactive chain, a brittle bind for cookie name (constructor-time only), one redundant/dead branch in setSessionId after PropertyMapper, and a few documentation/test-clarity nits. No blocking issues.

findings.title: Cookie name bound only at construction; runtime ServerProperties.name changes not reflected for resolve/expire
findings.detail: Constructor reads serverProperties.getReactive().getSession().getCookie().getName() once and pushes it to the parent via setCookieName(...). After that, resolveSessionIds()/expireSession() (inherited) and the override (which calls getCookieName()) all read the parent's stored field, not ServerProperties. Spring Boot also binds at startup, so behavior matches auto-config — but the resolver's setSessionId() reads other cookie attributes (path, domain, httpOnly, secure, sameSite, partitioned) live from ServerProperties on every call, while name is frozen at construction. The asymmetry can confuse a future maintainer who expects 'all flags live from ServerProperties' (this is exactly what the class-level comment promises: 'using ServerProperties for static flags'). In practice this is moot because env-driven properties are immutable post-startup, but the divergence deserves a note.
findings.suggestion: Either (a) read the cookie name live in setSessionId() too — String name = StringUtils.hasText(cookieProps.getName()) ? cookieProps.getName() : getCookieName(); — to make the data-flow uniform, or (b) add a one-line javadoc comment that documents the asymmetry: 'Name is propagated to the parent at construction so inherited resolve/expire use the same name as setSessionId; runtime mutation of ServerProperties.cookie.name is not supported, matching Boot auto-config.'

findings.title: PropertyMapper.alwaysApplyingWhenNonNull makes the secure(scheme==https)/sameSite("Lax") seed dead in this project's actual config
findings.detail: The override seeds path/httpOnly/secure/sameSite, then PropertyMapper.alwaysApplyingWhenNonNull() overlays whichever of {domain, path, httpOnly, secure, partitioned, sameSite} are non-null on cookieProps. application.properties (lines 14-16) always sets http-only, secure, and same-site (via env defaults SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE/SESSION_COOKIE_SAME_SITE), so for every real request the seed values for httpOnly/secure/sameSite are immediately overwritten — only the request-derived path and the parent's getCookieName() seed matter. The seed *does* protect a hypothetical configuration where these properties are removed entirely, which mirrors Boot's auto-config. So this is by design, but the comment claims the seed mirrors 'parent.initCookie sets defaults' — Spring's CookieWebSessionIdResolver.initCookie does the same scheme-based secure detection in the parent, so this isn't a faithful mirror so much as a re-implementation. Worth a clarifying comment so a future reader doesn't think the seed is ever reachable for httpOnly/secure/sameSite under this project's properties.
findings.suggestion: Either drop the seed for httpOnly/secure/sameSite (rely on PropertyMapper + the always-set config keys) and only seed path (which has no fallback in cookieProps when null), or add a comment: 'Seed values are reachable only when the corresponding ServerProperties key is null/unset (Boot's auto-config has the same fall-through). Under this project's application.properties the http-only/secure/same-site seeds are always overwritten; path is the only seed that survives because cookieProps.getPath() is null by default.'

findings.title: openSession publishes REMEMBER_ME_ATTR inside doOnNext on the session Mono; can be misread as ordering coupling
findings.detail: The exchange-attribute write does not depend on the WebSession emission — it only depends on `rememberMe` and `exchange`. Placing it as a second `.doOnNext(session -> exchange.getAttributes().put(...))` after the setMaxIdleTime doOnNext makes the dependency look intentional ('first TTL, then attribute'), but the resolver only reads the attribute at end-of-request when WebSessionManager flushes the session — there's no observable ordering between TTL set and attribute put. The current shape couples two semantically unrelated operations and creates a subtle gotcha: if a future change refactors the chain (e.g. moves attribute population earlier or extracts the session-fetch), it may inadvertently drop the attribute. The chosen placement also makes the second doOnNext silently no-op if the cached session Mono fails, which is exactly the wrong place to put an attribute that downstream cookie-writing depends on (though in practice openSession fails the whole pipeline if the session can't be fetched).
findings.suggestion: Pull the attribute write out of the chain: write it once before subscribing — `exchange.getAttributes().put(REMEMBER_ME_ATTR, Boolean.valueOf(rememberMe)); return exchange.getSession().doOnNext(session -> session.setMaxIdleTime(ttl)).then(securityContextRepository.save(exchange, context));` — and update the comment to 'Publish rememberMe to exchange attributes BEFORE the session pipeline so the resolver sees it on cookie flush regardless of session-fetch outcome.' This also matches the data-flow more honestly (attribute is request-scoped state, not session-scoped) and removes a reader's hesitation about the order's significance.

findings.title: Resolver lacks Javadoc on the public constant and the public class; relies on // block comments
findings.detail: REMEMBER_ME_ATTR is a public, cross-package contract (consumed by AuthService and tests). The class-level rationale is documented as a // comment block, which IDE Javadoc viewers don't render. Other security/auth classes in this project mix styles, but for a public extension point with a consumer in another package, a short Javadoc block on both the class and the constant would surface the contract in IDE tooling and Javadoc output without bloat.
findings.suggestion: Convert the leading // comment block on the class to /** ... */ Javadoc, and add a one-line Javadoc on REMEMBER_ME_ATTR: '/** ServerWebExchange attribute key. AuthService writes Boolean.TRUE/FALSE; setSessionId reads it on cookie flush. Absent or FALSE → session-only cookie. */'

findings.title: expireSession test does not exercise the inherited path/name seam under a custom cookie name
findings.detail: Scenario H verifies expireSession writes Max-Age=0 and empty value with the default 'SESSION' cookie name. The class spec depends on the constructor having propagated the cookie name to the parent so inherited expireSession uses it. With the default-name fixture, this is invisible — the parent's untouched default also produces 'SESSION'. A custom-name expire test (e.g. cookie name 'ALT' in propsWithDefaults) would lock in the constructor's setCookieName(...) propagation against silent regression. AC-8 covers it for setSessionId; expireSession deserves the same.
findings.suggestion: Add a one-line Scenario H' test: configure ServerProperties with name 'ALT', construct the resolver, call expireSession, assert exchange.getResponse().getCookies().getFirst("ALT") is not null and getMaxAge() is zero. Catches a regression where someone might drop the setCookieName(...) call in the constructor.

findings.title: Test fixture stubs Mockito getSession() with two consecutive Monos but openSession only consumes one — second mock is dead
findings.detail: mockExchangeWithSessions(WebSession preAuth, WebSession fresh) stubs when(exchange.getSession()).thenReturn(Mono.just(preAuth), Mono.just(fresh)). Per the comment in the rememberMe=true test (lines 331-333), AuthService.openSession only calls getSession() once per exchange (because in production it's a cached Mono). So the `fresh` parameter and the second Mono are never consumed by any test that uses this helper — they're documentation-only. Tests pass either way. This was useful during the pre-fix-broken-assertion era when verify(fresh) was wrong; now that the broken assertions are fixed, the second WebSession is dead weight.
findings.suggestion: Either drop the `fresh` parameter from mockExchangeWithSessions and from the call sites that no longer assert on it, or rename the helper to mockExchangeWithCachedSession(WebSession session) to reflect the actual behavior. Optional cleanup — current code is correct, just carrying historical baggage.
